Tuesdays

My grandmother could not cook. This is not a fond exaggeration; it is a matter
of record. She burned rice. She once served a chicken that was, in its centre,
still meaningfully raw, and when my grandfather pointed this out she said that
he was welcome to finish it in the garden with the other animals.

But on Tuesdays she made pancakes, and the pancakes were perfect.

Nobody could explain it. The same hands that could ruin boiled water produced,
every Tuesday at half past seven, a stack of pancakes so even and golden that
my mother once photographed them. She kept the photograph. It is on my fridge.

I asked her about it when I was nine. She was at the stove with her back to me,
and she said, without turning around, that it was not a mystery. She had made
pancakes every Tuesday since 1961. That was three thousand Tuesdays. Anyone
would be good at anything after three thousand Tuesdays.

I said that she cooked dinner every night and dinner was still bad.

She laughed so hard she had to sit down.

Then she said: dinner is a thing I have to do. Tuesday is a thing I chose.

She died in March, on a Wednesday, which I have always thought was poor timing
on her part. I inherited the pan. It is heavy and black and nothing sticks to
it, and I have made pancakes in it every Tuesday for eleven years.

I am not as good at it as she was. I have about two thousand Tuesdays left to
go.
